taste.summary: Hard, tight-grained and rather unappetising straight off the tree; after one to two months in store it turns crisp and juicy with a tart-sweet, wine-like and richly aromatic flavour, famously said to carry a hint of pineapple. The cut flesh browns quickly. A versatile apple for eating, pies, juice and cider.

One of the small group of pear-drop apples: a strong pear-drop flavour with lively, wine-like acidity and an aftertaste some growers liken to honey and pear. Growers disagree on texture, some finding the flesh soft and sponge-like with modest juice, others surprisingly juicy. Best kept until mid-winter, when it sweetens.

A sweet, pear-like russet with the classic English russet richness and enough acidity to stay lively; tasters rank it among the best-flavoured russets. The flesh is soft and slightly chewy, a little dry but less spongy than Egremont Russet, and it is a short keeper of two to three weeks.

Crisp, very juicy, fine-grained flesh with a brisk, roughly even sweet-tart balance and a rich aroma; one grower picks out vanilla notes. It keeps three months or more and holds its shape and tang when baked, which is why it is a classic North American pie apple.

Thin-skinned, juicy and just crisp enough, with a sweet flavour balanced by a fair tartness. Growers single out a delicate floral character, some likening it to lilac, and compare the overall taste with Mutsu or Crispin. Used for baking as well as eating.

Very sweet and honeyed with almost no acidity, aromatic and juicy; some tasters also find tropical-fruit overtones. The flesh is firm with a soft, Honeycrisp-like crunch. Admirers love its fragrance; those who like a sharp apple may find it flat.

Firm, fine-textured flesh that is not especially juicy but carries a rich, sweet, nutty and aromatic flavour with balancing acidity, close to Blenheim Orange and often compared with Ashmead's Kernel. One taster found a mango-like note after a week or so in store. Valued for flavour rather than crunch; it keeps its shape when cooked.

Tender, crisp yellowish flesh with a sweet, mildly acidic and highly aromatic flavour; nineteenth-century American writers rated it very good to best for winter eating. Modern opinion is more mixed, with at least one grower finding only a green, grassy taste.

Crisp, juicy, bright pink flesh with a very tart flavour lifted by just enough sweetness; tasters compare it to pink grapefruit or sweet lemonade, and one notes a touch of tannin. Almost a cooker in acidity, it makes attractive pink sauce and juice but keeps only two to three weeks.

Crisp, juicy and fairly tender, with an intense sweet flavour balanced by enough tartness; several tasters notice a floral scent reminiscent of roses. It shows its Cox ancestry and keeps three months or more without losing quality.

A small yellow apple whose firm, juicy, never-mealy flesh is sweet but lively, with a prominent musky, pineapple-like flavour that tasters also call sherbet-like; honeyed and nutty notes add richness. Best eaten within two or three weeks of picking.

Crisp, fairly juicy flesh with a sweet but noticeably tart flavour that varies from year to year; descriptions range from mild and Delicious-like to pleasantly sharp. Good fresh off the tree, it also holds its shape when baked, makes a pink-tinged sauce and keeps one to two months.

Crisp, juicy, firm yellow flesh that is Granny Smith-tart if picked a few weeks early, mellowing at full ripeness to a gentle tartness with sweetness beneath; one grower notes a pear-like flavour with a citrus bite. Unusually good for such an early apple but best eaten within a week or two; also good for sauce.

Fairly crisp, open-textured cream-yellow flesh that snaps cleanly, with a sweet flavour and good acidity much like Elstar; after a good summer it can carry a hint of strawberry. Juicy and pleasant rather than complex, and it keeps a few weeks.

Sweet, juicy flesh with a light crispness, very little acidity and only a faint aroma, sometimes likened to slightly over-ripe melon, under a thick, tough skin. Freshly picked fruit from a warm climate is refreshing, but stored supermarket fruit is often mealy and bland.

Crisp, very juicy, firm yellowish flesh with an aromatic, Cox-like flavour that is tangier and cleaner-tasting than Cox; most tasters find it refreshingly sharp, and it gains a honeyed sweetness only when fully ripe. A short keeper, best eaten within a week or so of picking.

Crisp and juicy straight from the tree, with a fresh, sweet flavour, a little zing and an overall mild character; some tasters detect an unusual note they put down to its crab-apple ancestry. It softens in storage within a few weeks and opinions vary, one grower finding it soft and flavourless. Dries well.
